raw_response:
I've been farming these 10 mu for 45 years now. I'm 65, went to middle school, and I know this land better than I know my own kitchen. My son and daughter-in-law work in the factory in Handan, so they send some money back, but that also means me and my wife do most of the field work ourselves. Six people in the household, but only two of us old folks really working the land day to day. We're not starving, but we're not rich either — every yuan I spend on inputs has to come back to me.

It's October now, so I need to get the wheat in the ground. I've been doing wheat-maize double cropping for as long as I can remember. The wheat pays for the year, and the maize is my margin. If one fails, the other usually saves me.

**Winter wheat** — I'll plant all 10.1 mu. I sow around October 10th, after the National Day holiday, when the soil is still warm enough for germination but not so hot that the seedlings get leggy. I use an improved variety, something like Jimai or Luyuan — I buy certified seed from the co-op, about 100 yuan per mu. I used to save my own seed, but the yield dropped too much. The extension fellow says to plant at 15 kg per mu, but I usually do a bit more, maybe 17-18 kg, just to be safe. I do rotary tillage before planting to break up the stubble from the maize.

For fertilizer, I put down compound fertilizer as my basal — about 40 jin per mu of 15-15-15, that's what I can afford and what the soil needs. Then at jointing, around Qingming Festival in early April, if the wheat looks a bit yellow, I'll topdress with urea, about 30 jin per mu. The extension guy said 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but I usually end up around 14 kg total — I can't afford to go too high, and honestly last year I did about this much and got 480 jin per mu, which is fine. I also need some phosphorus and potassium, so the compound fertilizer covers that. Total fertilizer cost runs me about 1600 yuan for wheat.

Irrigation is the big expense. I irrigate three times for wheat: once in late November or early December before the deep freeze, to protect the roots; once at jointing in March; and once at grain filling in May. Each time costs me about 40 yuan per mu for pumping, so that's over 1200 yuan just for water. But without it, the yield would drop by half — I've seen drought years. I use flood irrigation from my tube well, same as everyone.

For pesticides, I spray herbicide in early spring for the grassy weeds — they always come up. If I see aphids at the flag leaf stage, I'll spray insecticide too, but only if I see them. That's another 400 yuan or so.

Harvest is early June. I hire a combine, but my wife and I still work 4-5 days cutting, bundling, and hauling. I might hire one extra hand for 2 days if my back is acting up — 150 yuan per day.

I expect about 450 kg per mu this year. Last year was 480, but the spring was a bit dry and I'm getting conservative in my old age.

**Summer maize** — as soon as the wheat is out, usually by June 12th or 15th, I plant the maize. The window is tight — sometimes only 3 or 4 days. I don't have time to till again, so I no-till plant directly into the wheat stubble. Everyone in the village does it this way now. I buy hybrid seed — Denghai or something similar — at about 70 yuan per mu. It's expensive but worth it.

For maize fertilizer, I put compound fertilizer in the row at planting, about 25 jin per mu. Then at the big trumpet stage, around late July, I side-dress urea, about 25 jin per mu. Total nitrogen comes to about 11 kg per mu. The maize needs less fertilizer than wheat, and I don't push it too hard — if the rain is good, it'll yield fine. Phosphorus and potassium are modest, about 3 kg each per mu from the compound.

Irrigate twice for maize if it doesn't rain: once at jointing in late July, and once at filling in late August. Some years I get away with one if the monsoon is good. Pumping costs another 800 yuan or so.

Herbicide once before emergence or right after, and if the corn borer shows up in August, I spray insecticide. That's routine.

Harvest is late September. My wife and I work hard for 3-4 days, and I might hire one day of labor. Yield should be around 500 kg per mu if the weather cooperates. Last year I got 520, so I'm hoping for similar.

**My tradeoffs** — The big tension is between fertilizer and irrigation. I'd rather make sure I irrigate on time than buy more fertilizer, because water is what saves you in a dry year. I also have to keep some cash aside — my grandson needs school fees, and if someone gets sick, I can't have spent everything on the field. So I'm not maximizing anything. I'm doing what worked last year, what my neighbors do, and what I can pay for.
